board_content.text: Complex roots travel in mirror-image pairs
If a polynomial has real coefficients and $p+iq$ ($q\neq0$) is a root, so is $p-iq$.
The proof conjugates the whole equation; $\bar a=a$ etc. because the coefficients are real.
Holds ONLY for real coefficients — with complex ones it fails.
So with real coefficients you only ever find one complex root; the other is its conjugate.
Change to complex coefficients and the symmetry breaks: roots can be any two numbers.
Assuming conjugate pairs with complex coefficients is the classic conceptual error.

segments_english.text: The conjugate-root theorem is the most conceptually important idea in this subtopic, and its condition is easy to forget.
It says: if a quadratic, indeed any polynomial, has real coefficients, and p plus i q is a root with q nonzero, then its mirror image p minus i q is forced to be a root too.
Here's why. Suppose a z squared plus b z plus c is zero at some root. Take the conjugate of the entire equation.

Conjugation distributes over sums and products, and because the coefficients are real, a bar equals a, b bar equals b, c bar equals c. So the conjugated equation reads a z bar squared plus b z bar plus c equals zero, meaning z bar is also a root.
And this is the whole point: the proof used a bar equals a, which is exactly where real coefficients are required. With complex coefficients the theorem simply fails.
The practical upside for real coefficients is lovely: you only ever need to find one complex root. The other one is automatically its conjugate, for free.
But change the coefficients to complex and that symmetry breaks completely. The two roots can be any two complex numbers, with no mirror relationship at all.
So the classic conceptual error, and a favourite exam trap, is assuming roots come in conjugate pairs even when the coefficients are not real. Always check the coefficients first.

segments_hinglish.text: Conjugate-root theorem is subtopic ka sabse conceptually important idea hai, aur iski condition bhoolna aasan hai.
Ye kehta hai: agar ek quadratic, dar-asal koi bhi polynomial, ke real coefficients hon, aur p plus i q ek root ho with q nonzero, to iska mirror image p minus i q bhi root hone par majboor hai.
Kyun. Maano a z squared plus b z plus c kisi root par zero hai. Poori equation ka conjugate lo.

Conjugation sums aur products par distribute karti hai, aur kyunki coefficients real hain, a bar barabar a, b bar barabar b, c bar barabar c. To conjugated equation banti hai a z bar squared plus b z bar plus c equals zero, matlab z bar bhi ek root hai.
Aur yehi poora point hai: proof ne a bar barabar a use kiya, jo bilkul wahi jagah hai jahan real coefficients zaroori hain. Complex coefficients ke saath theorem bas fail ho jaata hai.
Real coefficients ke liye practical faayda pyaara hai: aapko sirf ek complex root nikaalna hota hai. Doosra apne aap uska conjugate hai, muft mein.
Par coefficients ko complex banao aur wo symmetry poori tarah toot jaati hai. Do roots koi bhi do complex numbers ho sakte hain, bina kisi mirror relationship ke.
To classic conceptual error, aur favourite exam trap, ye maan lena hai ki roots conjugate pairs mein aate hain chahe coefficients real na hon. Hamesha pehle coefficients check karo.
